open-question.question: The mission's goal opens with a hands-on check of what Claude Desktop accepts from outside (a prompt, a folder, a model, an effort, a permission mode), and most of the feature's design hinges on what that check finds. Is the check run before the mission's remaining open questions are answered, with its findings written into the relevant starting state, or as the mission's first task after task derivation, with the decisions made beforehand written to hold for whichever outcome it finds?
open-question.alternative: The whole hands-on check (the `claude://code/new` link and the `claude --desktop` option, each tried for a prefilled or already-sent prompt, the folder the session opens on, and any model, effort, or permission mode it takes) is run now, by the person at the machine, outside any task, before the recommendation pass and the answer sweep run over the mission's questions; its findings are written into `## Relevant starting state` beside the static reading of Claude Desktop 5.11492.5 already there, and every open question is then recommended and answered against observed behaviour. If no prompt can be passed, the mission stops at that point, before any decision is recorded. Every decision that hinges on Desktop's behaviour (which opening mechanism, what happens to uncarried values, the over-long prompt, the stop conditions) is made against what Desktop was seen to do rather than against a guess, so no decision has to be written conditionally and the stop, if it comes, costs no decision work at all. The check is work outside the workflow's steps: no skill runs it, and since `specify-mission-starting-state` explores again only when `since` prints commits past its anchor, the findings reach the section by a hand edit or through a commit of the check's record that moves the ground (where that record lives is the sibling question on the check's record); the whole preparation waits until a person sits down with Claude Desktop, and picks formed before the findings land would need stripping.

The full hands-on check runs before answering, as in a pre-answer check with its findings written into `## Relevant starting state`, but only the questions whose answer hinges on its outcome wait for it; the questions that hold whatever it finds (how Desktop is selected for an action, the Harnesses row, the listing texts, the send feedback) are recommended and answered now, each through a single-question answer skill rather than the whole-mission sweep. Preparation keeps moving on the outcome-independent questions while the check waits for a person at the machine, and the decisions that do hinge on Desktop are still made against observed behaviour. Sorting the questions into dependent and independent is a judgment that can miss a dependency (a selection mechanism may yet hinge on whether Desktop takes a folder), the answer sweep cannot be used while some picks must be held, and a stop after the check leaves the independent decisions already recorded as wasted work.

Only the part of the check that decides whether the mission goes on and which mechanism can carry a prompt (does a prompt arrive through the link and through `claude --desktop`, prefilled or sent, and on which folder) is run now and written into `## Relevant starting state` before answering; the rest (whether `claude --desktop` takes a model, an effort, or a permission mode, how a long prompt behaves in practice) is the mission's first task after task derivation, with the decisions it touches written to hold for either outcome. The stop condition and the facts most decisions turn on are settled before any decision is made, at the cost of a short check, while the details whose outcome only shapes what the feature carries stay inside the task pipeline with a verified bar of their own. The line between the two parts is drawn before anyone has seen Desktop, so a fact left to the task may prove to decide a question already answered, and the decisions over the deferred part must still be written conditionally; the pre-answer part shares the hand-edit route into the starting state of a full pre-answer check.

The full hands-on check runs before answering, its findings written into `## Relevant starting state` and every question answered against them, and task derivation also places a first task that repeats the check against the Claude Desktop version installed when execution starts, stopping the run where the findings no longer hold. Decisions are made against observed behaviour, and the feature is still built against the behaviour that holds when it is built, which matters for an application updated as often as Claude Desktop (its static reading names a build number, 5.11492.5, not a stable interface). The check is run twice, the second time by a task that needs a person to watch Desktop (an unattended `complete-all-tasks` run cannot see whether a prompt arrived prefilled), and a changed finding at that point means revising recorded decisions after task derivation, which the workflow has no step for beyond revert and re-answer.

No check runs before answering: every open question is recommended and answered now against the static reading in `## Relevant starting state`, each decision that hinges on Desktop's behaviour written to hold for whichever outcome the check finds (a conditional pick of mechanism, values, and stop), and the hands-on check is the mission's first task after task derivation, its outcome choosing among the prepared branches and, where no prompt can be passed, stopping the mission there. The check runs inside the workflow, as a task with a derived and verified acceptance bar recorded in its `Task-completion:` commit, and preparation proceeds at once through the ordinary review, annotation, and answer sweep with no hand edit of the starting state. Conditional decisions are harder to write and to derive tasks from, every branch the check does not take is decision work spent for nothing, a stop after derivation leaves a task list holding feature tasks that must be removed before `finish-mission` will run, and the task needs a person to observe Desktop, so it cannot run in an unattended `complete-all-tasks` pass; how far the stop reaches depends on the sibling question on the check's stop conditions.

open-question.question: Where are the findings of the hands-on check of Claude Desktop recorded so that they outlive the mission's directory (the day, the Claude Desktop version checked, what was passed, and what arrived), both when the mission goes on and when it stops because no prompt can be passed?
open-question.alternative: No home outside the mission, in either outcome: the findings (the day, the Claude Desktop version checked, what was passed, and what arrived) are written into the mission's own requirements.md, in whichever section the check's timing puts them, and the Mission-finish: commit's summary body carries them as bullets, whether the mission finishes with the feature in place or stops after the check because no prompt can be passed. They outlive the directory as history only, read back through the missions tool's summary, record, and show at the finish commit and its parent. Adds no file, convention, or second copy: the finish commit already is the record of a finished mission, finish-mission writes it the same way in both outcomes, and the record and show queries already serve it to every later goal discussion and starting-state read. Nothing in the tree says what Desktop took or on which version, so someone editing the Desktop harness code, or re-checking after a Desktop update, finds the findings only by searching history, and the finish summary's bullets tend to compress them, the full detail standing only at the finish commit's parent; where the findings first land inside requirements.md depends on the Hands-on check timing question.

In the outcome where the mission goes on, the findings are kept as a dated comment block in the extension's source beside the Claude Desktop harness entry (in src/harnessCheck.ts, next to HARNESSES), naming the day, the Desktop version checked, what was passed, and what arrived, which a later re-check updates in place, mirroring the dated hands-on block each host's scripts/hosts/<host>/settings.toml carries in its header comment. In the outcome where the mission stops, no harness code is written, so the findings go into the mission's own record and its Mission-finish: summary body as under the mission-record option. Follows the repository's own convention for recording a hands-on check, and puts the findings exactly where a later editor of the Desktop code reads, with an established habit of updating the block when the application is checked again. Gives the two outcomes two different homes, so a stopped mission's findings are reachable from history only, which is where a later attempt at the same feature most needs them, and the extension has no such comment convention yet, so it is a new practice carried into TypeScript source rather than a reused one.

In both outcomes the findings are written to one tracked maintainer-facing document outside the mission directory and outside the VSIX (a note under ideas/, or a section of gurita-vscode/BUILDING.md), holding the day, the Desktop version checked, what was passed, and what arrived, and, when the mission stops, why it stopped; the Mission-finish: summary points at it rather than repeating it. One in-tree home whatever the outcome, so a stopped mission leaves a readable account standing exactly where a later attempt, or a re-check after a Desktop update, would start, without anyone having to know which finish commit to read. Creates a document no tool, skill, or reader is bound to, which ages silently as Claude Desktop updates, and fits neither candidate home cleanly: ideas/ holds design drafts that precede a mission and BUILDING.md documents the build.

In the outcome where the mission goes on, gurita-vscode/USAGE.md, the documentation the goal already brings up to date, states what Claude Desktop accepts from outside as observed by the check, stamped with the day and the Desktop version checked, together with what was passed and what arrived. In the outcome where the mission stops, USAGE.md gains nothing and the findings go into the mission's own record and its Mission-finish: summary body as under the mission-record option. The findings reach the people who use the feature, version-stamped, in a file the mission edits anyway, so a person can tell whether their own Desktop version is the one whose behaviour the documentation describes. Puts maintainer-facing test detail (what exactly was passed) into the installed extension's user reference, and like the dated-block option leaves the stopped outcome with no in-tree record; what USAGE.md says of values Desktop does not carry also touches the Uncarried line values question.

In both outcomes the findings are written into the project's CLAUDE.md, the context file every later session reads, as finish-mission's lasting-change edit riding in the Mission-finish: commit: the day, the Desktop version checked, what was passed, what arrived, and, when the mission stops, why Claude Desktop is not a harness. Every later session reads it unprompted, so a later proposal to add Desktop again meets the stopped mission's reason before any work starts, and the edit rides the finish step that already writes lasting changes, in both outcomes alike. Runs against the repository's practice of keeping tool versions and observed-behaviour facts out of the context file, which records rationale only and is already very long, and a version-stamped observation there goes stale at the next Desktop update with nothing prompting its revision.

open-question.question: The goal stops the mission when the hands-on check finds that no prompt can be passed to Claude Desktop. Which other findings, if any, stop it the same way: a session that cannot be opened on the project's folder, a Desktop session in which the Gurita plugin's `/gurita:` skills are not available, or none?
open-question.alternative: No finding beyond the goal's own stops the mission. A session that cannot be opened on the project's folder does not stop it, and the feature opens the Desktop session wherever Desktop puts it, leaving the person to move it to the project's folder. A Desktop session without the `/gurita:` skills does not stop it either, and the feature sends the prompt as the line carries it, leaving the person to make the plugin available in Desktop. The stop list stays exactly the goal's: no prompt can be passed. It keeps the goal as written and lets the mission ship whatever the check finds short of the one stated failure, so a partial result (the prompt arrives but the folder or the skills need a hand step) still gives the person Desktop's visual and sound artifacts, which is the reason the harness exists. The feature can ship as a button that opens a session where the skill invocation in its prompt does nothing, or one working on the wrong folder, so the action the person clicked is not the action that runs. What the person is told about that hand step falls to the questions on the Desktop Harnesses row, send feedback, and harness availability, and the feature is only as usable as those answers make it.

Two findings stop the mission: no prompt can be passed, or no session can be opened on the project's folder (neither the `claude://code/new` link's `folder` parameter nor the `claude` CLI's `--desktop` option puts the session there). A Desktop session without the `/gurita:` skills does not stop it, and the feature sends the prompt as the line carries it, leaving the person to make the plugin available in Desktop. Every Gurita action reads and writes a mission inside the project, so a session on another folder cannot do the work at all and is likely to write into the wrong tree, while missing skills are a one-time setup step the person can fix in Desktop and then rely on. It ships a feature whose prompts invoke skills Desktop may not have, so a fresh Desktop install sends a `/gurita:` prompt that resolves to nothing until the person installs the plugin there, with nothing in the extension's checks today able to tell (every Harnesses check assumes a CLI). Whether that gap is shown falls to the Desktop Harnesses row question.

Two findings stop the mission: no prompt can be passed, or the `/gurita:` skills are not available in the Desktop session opened (Desktop does not load the Gurita plugin copy Claude Code has, and offers no way to install it). A session that cannot be opened on the project's folder does not stop it, and the feature opens the session wherever Desktop puts it, leaving the person to pick the project's folder in Desktop. Every action the harness serves is a `/gurita:` skill invocation, so without the skills the prompt is plain text and the feature does nothing Gurita-specific, while a folder the person picks once in Desktop's own picker is a small hand step that leaves the action intact. It ships a feature that can open the session on a folder other than the project's, so until the person moves it the skill runs against the wrong tree or finds no mission, and a person who misses the step gets a session that writes outside the project. Whether the folder can be reached at all from a remote window is the harness availability question's, and this option leaves that case to it.

Three findings stop the mission the same way: no prompt can be passed, no session can be opened on the project's folder, or the `/gurita:` skills are not available in the Desktop session. The feature is built only when the check finds a session that opens on the project's folder, with the prompt prefilled, and with the skills it invokes available; otherwise the mission stops at the check and records why. The feature ships only when a click does what the action promises, the named skill running on the project's mission, so no button opens a session that silently cannot do its job and no hand step has to be documented or detected. It is the strictest bar and the likeliest to end the mission with nothing built, even where a hand step (picking the folder once, installing the plugin in Desktop once) would have made the feature work, which gives up the visual and sound artifacts the goal is after for a gap the person could close themselves.

No stop list beyond the goal's is fixed now. The check runs, and a finding that the session cannot be opened on the project's folder or that the `/gurita:` skills are not available is weighed when it is found, as a goal revision or a new open question, deciding then whether the mission stops, narrows, or goes on with a hand step. The decision is made against what Desktop actually does rather than against guesses, since nothing about how a folder or the plugin reaches a Desktop session has been observed, and a finding nobody foresaw (the session opening but reading another plugin copy, for instance) gets the same treatment as the two named ones. It leaves the mission's end condition open, so the decisions taken before the check cannot be written to hold for every outcome, and it works only where the check's findings reach a point at which a question can still be asked; whether they do is the hands-on check timing question's, and run as a task after derivation the check leaves no such point without stopping the task run.

open-question.question: Two ways of opening a Claude Desktop session from outside are known and neither has been tried: the `claude://code/new` link, which takes a prompt and a folder, and the `claude` CLI's `--desktop` option. Which does Gurita for VS Code use to send an action to Claude Desktop where the hands-on check finds that both pass a prompt?
open-question.alternative: The `claude://code/new` link only, the `claude` CLI not used: Gurita builds the link with the action's prompt, its placeholder values written into the text, as `q` and the project's root folder as `folder`, and hands it to `vscode.env.openExternal`, the extension's first call of that API. It depends on Claude Desktop alone, the scheme Claude.app registers and its own Finder service uses, with no CLI on the shell's path, and it starts no child process: VS Code's own API opens the link on the person's machine, including from a remote window. Placeholder values live only in the terminal's `GURITA_*` variables today, so a new function has to write them into the prompt text. The link cuts the prompt at 14,336 characters and names no model, effort, or permission mode, so the line's flags cannot travel with it. The only sign of failure is openExternal's boolean. In a remote window the folder is a remote path, so this option's reach depends on where the harness is offered, which the availability question decides.

The same `claude://code/new` link, with the prompt's values written in and the project's root as `folder`, passed to the operating system's opener (`open` on macOS, `xdg-open` on Linux) as an `execFile` child, the way the extension already runs its git and Python reads. The `claude` CLI is not used. The opener's exit status and stderr are a failure signal Gurita can read, for example no application handling the `claude` scheme, and the extension keeps its existing pattern of `execFile` children with no openExternal call. It has the link's costs: a new function to write values into the prompt, the 14,336-character cut, and no model, effort, or permission mode. The opener also runs on the extension host, which in a remote window is the remote machine, where no Claude.app runs, so where it works depends on the availability question. Each platform needs its own command.

The `claude` CLI's `--desktop` option only. The action's one interactive line runs as today, through the bundled runner in a terminal at the project root, with `--desktop` added to its `claude` command and no run tracked. The link is not used. The line's text stays whole. The shell expands the `GURITA_*` variables, so no function writes values into the prompt and no 14,336-character link cut applies. The line's `--model`, `--effort`, and bypass flag ride on the same command wherever the CLI forwards them, and the folder is the terminal's working directory. A VS Code terminal still opens, which the goal sets the Desktop session against, and the runner's run tracking has to be bypassed for this one kind of send. It needs `claude` on the session shell's path. Nobody has observed whether `--desktop` without `--continue` or `--resume` opens a new session with the prompt in place.

The `claude` CLI's `--desktop` option only, run by the extension itself as a background child of the session shell at the project root. The line's `claude` command gets `--desktop` added, and the `GURITA_*` values are set in the child's environment. No terminal opens and the link is not used. No terminal opens, yet the shell still expands the values and the line's own flags travel with it. The child's exit status and stderr give a failure signal, and there is no link length cut. It adds a new kind of child process. Nobody knows whether the CLI exits once it hands off to Desktop or stays running, and it needs `claude` on the session shell's path. In a remote window it runs on the remote host, so where it works depends on the availability question. Whether `--desktop` alone opens a new session with the prompt has not been observed.

Both mechanisms, chosen per send. When the harness check finds `claude` on the session shell's path, Gurita runs `--desktop` as a background child of the session shell at the project root. Otherwise it opens the `claude://code/new` link, with the values written into the prompt and the project's root as `folder`, through `vscode.env.openExternal`. Desktop is reachable for a person who has Claude.app but no CLI. Wherever the CLI is present, the send keeps the line's flags and avoids the link's prompt cut. Two code paths to build, test, and document, with different carried values and different failure signals. The same action can then open differently on two machines, for example with or without the line's model, and the person cannot tell which route was taken.

No mechanism is fixed now. The choice is left to the hands-on check under one stated rule: use whichever mechanism, when tried, also carries more of the project's folder, the model, the effort, and the permission mode, and leaves the prompt prefilled rather than already sent. On a tie, use the link. The choice rests on what Claude Desktop is seen to do rather than on a static reading of its bundle and the CLI's help text, which so far has observed nothing that either route delivers. The questions on feedback, over-long prompts, the Harnesses row, and remote availability are each shaped by the mechanism, so they stay unsettled or must be written to hold for either. How much that costs depends on when the check runs, which the timing question decides.

open-question.question: How does a person select Claude Desktop for an action in Gurita for VS Code, given that no action carries a harness setting of its own, that a line's harness is today the command the line opens with, and that the variants of one action can differ in whether they are a single interactive line?

In which windows does Gurita for VS Code offer the Claude Desktop harness: everywhere the extension runs, or only where Claude Desktop can reach the project's folder? The extension runs on macOS, on Linux, and in remote windows (Remote-WSL, SSH), where the project's folder is not a path an application on the person's own machine can open, and it stays inert on native Windows.

What does Claude Desktop's row under Harnesses in the Settings window hold, given that the three existing rows each check a CLI (the command found in the shell, a Gurita plugin copy read through the CLI's plugin listing, that copy's version against the packaged one) and carry Install and Update controls: which of those checks does the row make for an application that is no CLI, and does it carry Install and Update controls?

When an action is sent to Claude Desktop and Desktop takes no model, effort, or permission mode from outside, what becomes of the `--model`, `--effort`, and bypass-permission values the action's line carries: are they dropped without sign, or is the person shown, in the Settings window or on the action's button, that the Desktop session will not carry them?

What does Gurita for VS Code do when an action's prompt, with the values the person typed written into it (a goal, an issue description, a question), is longer than Claude Desktop accepts from outside, the `claude://code/new` link cutting its prompt at 14,336 characters?

Sending an action to Claude Desktop is fire-and-forget, with no run tracked. What does the person see in VS Code after the click: anything at all on a send that went out, and what on a send that failed, such as Claude Desktop not being installed or the link not being handled?

The goal names `gurita-vscode/USAGE.md` as the documentation the mission brings up to date. Do the texts outside it that name the three harnesses (the listing `README.md` and the manifest's description and keywords) also come to name Claude Desktop in this mission, which makes no extension release?
